lead: CAN (Controller Area Network) is the bus most ECUs in a car use: a two-wire, multi-master broadcast bus in which every node hears every frame and each frame carries a number that names its content. When two nodes start together, a dominant 0 overrides a recessive 1, so the lower identifier wins and its frame goes on undamaged. Classic CAN carries 0 to 8 data bytes at up to 1 Mbit/s; CAN FD (flexible data rate) keeps the arbitration and adds a faster data phase and up to 64 bytes.
prereq: You need topology, OSI layers and bus classes.

sections.h3: The two wires and bit-wise arbitration

blocks.text: Each node has a CAN controller that builds and checks frames and a transceiver that drives the twisted pair, CAN_H and CAN_L. In high-speed CAN (ISO 11898-2), a recessive bit (logic 1) leaves both wires at about 2.5 V, so the difference is 0 V. A dominant bit (logic 0) drives CAN_H to about 3.5 V and CAN_L to about 1.5 V, a difference of about 2 V. A 120 Ω resistor at each end of the trunk stops reflections; seen from the wires, the two are in parallel, so a healthy bus measures 60 Ω between CAN_H and CAN_L with the power off.
If one node drives dominant while another leaves the bus recessive, the bus is dominant. The wire acts like an AND gate on the logic levels (wired-AND). Arbitration uses this:

items: The bus is idle (recessive). Every node with a frame waiting sends the start-of-frame bit, a dominant 0.
Each node sends its identifier, most significant bit first, and reads the bus after every bit.
A node that sent recessive 1 but reads dominant 0 has lost. It stops sending at once and becomes a receiver of the other frame.
The node that never saw a difference wins and finishes its frame. The loser tries again when the bus is next idle.

blocks.text: No bit of the winning frame is damaged, so this is non-destructive arbitration, and a lower identifier means a higher priority: brake and engine messages get low identifiers.

sections.h3: Classic CAN frame, bit stuffing and error handling

blocks.text: A standard data frame has these fields, in order:

head: Field
Bits
Purpose
rows: Dominant start bit; nodes synchronise on it
Names the content and sets the priority
Dominant: data frame; recessive: remote frame
Cyclic redundancy check over the frame
Receivers that found the frame correct drive it dominant
Recessive gap before the next frame

blocks.text: Bit stuffing keeps edges on the wire for synchronisation: after five equal bits in a row the transmitter adds one bit of the opposite value, and every receiver removes it. Stuffing covers the bits from SOF to the end of the CRC sequence.

Each node checks for five errors: bit (a sender reads back a different bit, outside arbitration), stuff (six equal bits), CRC, form (a fixed bit such as a delimiter is wrong) and ACK (no receiver acknowledged). A node that finds one sends an error frame of six dominant bits, so every node discards the frame, and the sender repeats it. Each node counts its errors in a transmit error counter (TEC) and a receive error counter (REC). It is error active while both are 127 or less, error passive when either exceeds 127 (it may only send a recessive error flag), and bus-off when TEC exceeds 255 (it stops sending altogether). This fault confinement keeps one faulty node from blocking the bus.

blocks.where: SP is the sample point as a fraction of one bit; a bit has N time quanta: one sync quantum, PROP for propagation delay, PHASE1 and PHASE2 either side of the sample point, N = 1 + PROP + PHASE1 + PHASE2. About 75 to 87.5 per cent is usual.

sections.h3: CAN FD: same arbitration, faster data

blocks.text: CAN FD keeps the identifier and arbitration rules, so priority works exactly as before, and changes the control field. RTR becomes RRS, always dominant, because CAN FD has no remote frames; IDE stays. Then come FDF (FD format, recessive in an FD frame), a reserved bit, BRS (bit rate switch: recessive means the data phase runs at the fast rate) and ESI (error state indicator: shows whether the sender is error passive).

DLC 0 to 8 means that many bytes; 9 to 15 mean 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48 and 64 bytes. The CRC is 17 bits up to 16 bytes and 21 bits above. A typical setting is arbitration at 500 kbit/s and a data phase at 2 Mbit/s. A classic controller cannot share a bus with FD frames: when it reads the recessive FDF bit where it expects the dominant r0, it raises a form error and destroys the FD frame. Every controller on an FD bus must therefore be FD-capable; the wires, transceivers rated for the fast rate and 120 Ω terminations stay the same.

examples.question: Nodes A and B start arbitration at the same moment. A sends standard identifier 0x123 and B sends 0x121. Which node wins, at which identifier bit, and what does the loser do?
steps: Write the 11 bits, most significant first (bit 10 down to bit 0): A = 001 0010 0011, B = 001 0010 0001.
Bits 10 down to 2 are the same in both (001 0010 00), so both nodes read back what they sent.
At bit 1, A sends recessive 1 and B sends dominant 0. The bus reads 0.
A sent 1 but read 0, so A has lost. It stops sending and receives B's frame. Bit 0 is 1 in both; only B is still sending.
B finishes its frame undamaged. A sends its frame when the bus is next idle.
examples.answer: B (0x121, decimal 289) wins at identifier bit 1, because it has a dominant 0 there and A has a recessive 1; A becomes a receiver and retries after B's frame.

examples.question: A standard CAN data frame carries 8 data bytes on a 500 kbit/s bus. (a) How many bits does it have without stuffing, counting the 3-bit interframe space? (b) The worst case adds one stuff bit for every 4 bits after the first in the stuffed region; how many bits is that? (c) How long does the frame occupy the bus in each case? (d) What is the useful data rate with no stuffing?
steps: Fixed bits from SOF to EOF: 1 + 11 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 15 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 7 = 44 bits, plus 8 × 8 = 64 data bits: 108 bits. With the interframe space: 108 + 3 = 111 bits.
Stuffed region (SOF to end of CRC): 1 + 11 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 64 + 15 = 98 bits. Worst-case stuff bits = (98 − 1) ÷ 4 = 24.25, so 24 bits.
Bit time at 500 kbit/s = 1 ÷ 500 000 = 2 µs. No stuffing: 111 × 2 µs = 222 µs. Worst case: 135 × 2 µs = 270 µs.
Useful data rate with no stuffing: 64 data bits every 222 µs = 64 ÷ 0.000222 = 288 288 bit/s, about 288 kbit/s, which is 64 ÷ 111 = 57.7 per cent of 500 kbit/s.
examples.answer: (a) 111 bits; (b) 135 bits; (c) 222 µs and 270 µs; (d) about 288 kbit/s of data, 57.7 per cent of the bit rate.

traps: The lower identifier wins, because dominant is 0 and recessive is 1. Writing "the higher priority number wins" loses the mark.
CAN FD switches only the data phase to the fast rate (BRS); arbitration and ACK stay at the nominal rate, so priority works as in classic CAN.
In CAN FD a DLC above 8 is a code, not a byte count: 9 means 12 bytes, 10 means 16 and 15 means 64.
Bus-off follows TEC above 255; error passive follows TEC or REC above 127. Do not swap the two limits.

quiz.q: Which logic level is dominant on CAN, and what are the CAN_H and CAN_L voltages for it?
quiz.a: Logic 0 is dominant: CAN_H about 3.5 V and CAN_L about 1.5 V, a difference of about 2 V. Recessive leaves both near 2.5 V.

quiz.q: Why is CAN arbitration called non-destructive?
quiz.a: The loser stops at the bit where it sees a dominant 0 against its recessive 1, before it can corrupt anything, so the winning frame is received intact and no bus time is wasted.

quiz.q: Nodes send identifiers 0x200 and 0x204 together. Which wins and at which bit?
quiz.a: 0x200 = 010 0000 0000 and 0x204 = 010 0000 0100. They first differ at bit 2, where 0x200 sends 0 and 0x204 sends 1, so 0x200 wins.

quiz.q: Find the sample point if N = 16 time quanta, PROP = 7, PHASE1 = 4 and PHASE2 = 4.
quiz.a: SP = (1 + 7 + 4) ÷ 16 = 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75, so the bus is sampled at 75 per cent of each bit.

quiz.q: A technician measures 120 Ω between CAN_H and CAN_L with the power off. What is wrong?
quiz.a: A healthy bus has two 120 Ω terminators in parallel, which gives 60 Ω. Reading 120 Ω means one terminator is missing or the trunk is broken between them.

quiz.q: Why does CAN FD need a stronger CRC and why can a classic node not stay on an FD bus?
quiz.a: A frame of up to 64 bytes has many more bits that can be hit by noise, so a 17- or 21-bit CRC keeps the chance of an undetected error low. A classic node reads the recessive FDF bit as a form error and sends an error frame, destroying every FD frame.

beyond: Not for the exam. CAN XL raises the payload to 2048 bytes and the data phase to about 10 Mbit/s for zonal networks. Partial networking lets an ECU sleep until a frame with its own wake-up identifier arrives. Search for CAN XL, partial networking and SecOC (message authentication).
